title: Soil and shale under the western GTA | GTA Helical Piles
description: What the Ontario Geological Survey maps show under Toronto, Peel, Halton, Hamilton, Guelph and Niagara, and what each soil and rock unit means for a pile.
h1: Shale, clay and till: what is under your deck
lede: For homeowners and deck builders from Toronto to St. Catharines who want to know what a helical pile will meet under their yard. We queried the Ontario Geological Survey's surface and bedrock map services at sixteen points across our area and explain each recurring unit in plain language: what it is, how a pile behaves in it, and why one street's engineering does not carry to the next.

sections.heading: How we read the ground: two provincial maps
paragraphs: Two Ontario Geological Survey datasets describe the ground under every town we serve. Surficial Geology of Southern Ontario (MRD 128-REV) maps the loose material left by glaciers, lakes and rivers, compiled from 125 maps mostly at 1:50,000. Paleozoic Geology of Southern Ontario (MRD 219) maps the bedrock beneath it at the same scale. Both are public ArcGIS feature services: one coordinate returns the unit at that spot.

The table lists the sixteen points we queried on 2026-09-25. Each row is one coordinate, not a municipality; the unit can change within a few hundred metres near creeks and the old shoreline. A 1:50,000 map cannot show a buried channel or the fill beside a foundation, and neither dataset gives depth to bedrock. Treat the table as a starting hypothesis, not the engineer's determination.

sections.heading: Halton Till and the Peel clay plain
paragraphs: The most common answer inland is unit 5d, clay to silt-textured till derived from lake sediment or shale. Regional reports call it Halton Till. A Peel Region geotechnical desktop study describes it as dense, sandy to silty clay till, clast poor and reddish brown, typically 3 to 6 m thick but locally 15 to 30 m. Brampton, Bolton, Mississauga City Centre and inland Oakville sit on it.

Over parts of Peel and Halton a skin of lake clay lies on the till. The Peel Plain is a level to undulating tract of clayey soil covering about 800 square kilometres of York, Peel and Halton, the bed of glacial Lake Peel, which pooled between the ice front, the Niagara Escarpment and the Trafalgar Moraine. Old Milton returned unit 8b, silt and clay with flow till; Hamilton Mountain unit 8a.

For a pile, dense clay till is dependable ground: torque climbs steadily and the pile reaches its design value without surprises. Installation torque is recorded on every pile and correlated to capacity using the torque tables in the pile's CCMC evaluation report. Two cautions from OGS Report 257: the till was preconsolidated by glacial overriding, so the weathered top metre can read low, and the lake silts above it may be frost-susceptible.

sections.heading: Lake Iroquois sands, outwash gravels and the Oak Ridges Moraine
paragraphs: When the ice retreated, an enlarged Lake Ontario called glacial Lake Iroquois stood roughly 30 to 45 m above today's lake. Its waves cut a shorecliff and dropped bars of sand and gravel along a strip 3 to 5 km wide inland of the present shore; in Toronto, Davenport Road follows it. Downtown Toronto, Burlington, Hamilton lower city, Ancaster and St. Catharines all returned unit 9, coarse glaciolacustrine sand and gravel.

Two other granular units appear north and west. Georgetown and downtown Guelph returned unit 7b, gravelly glaciofluvial river and delta deposits. Palgrave in Caledon returned unit 6, ice-contact stratified sand and gravel: the Oak Ridges Moraine, primarily sand and gravel rather than clay till. North York returned unit 5b, a sandy silt till closer to these than to Halton Till.

Granular ground changes how we prove a pile. CCMC report 13675-R states that where the pile is installed in granular material exceeding 200 mm in diameter the relationship between torque and allowable load is not as predictable, and the allowable loads have to be confirmed by on-site load tests under a geotechnical engineer holding a licence. Torque can rise in a gravel bar and fall in loose sand beneath.

sections.heading: Queenston and Georgian Bay shale: the bedrock under the lake plain
paragraphs: Below the till and beach sand, from Toronto to St. Catharines, the bedrock is Ordovician shale. MRD 219 describes the Georgian Bay Formation as interbedded grey-green to dark grey shale with calcareous siltstone to limestone, and the Queenston Formation as red shale and siltstone with minor green shale and limestone interbeds. Toronto, Mississauga and Bolton are on Georgian Bay; Brampton, Milton, Georgetown, Burlington, Hamilton lower city, Grimsby and St. Catharines on Queenston.

Shale is usually buried, but not always. OGS mapping shows bedrock at or near surface in the Sixteen Mile Creek and Bronte Creek valleys in Oakville, a Queenston outcrop is exposed at Bronte Creek just south of the QEW, and the Lake Iroquois shorecliff west of Clarkson in Mississauga is cut in shale. Report 257 says bedrock is commonly shallow below the Trafalgar Moraine. Creek-side lots and the old shorecliff are where we expect rock.

A pile that reaches hard shale before its design torque hits refusal: rotation without advance. Magnum's bulletin on bedrock end bearing explains that a sharp soil-to-rock transition can make the pile spin out, after which the torque correlation is no longer valid; its example specification lists the responses: record refusal, back out and re-advance with less crowd, resize to fewer or smaller helices, pre-drill a pilot hole matching the shaft, or excavate a shallow obstruction. GoliathTech relocates the pile where the layout allows. The engineer decides, from our torque record, whether the pile is accepted. Our illustrative deck range is $325 to $475 per pile installed; pre-drilling adds time, and the firm price follows the site review.

sections.heading: Escarpment dolostone: Hamilton Mountain, Ancaster and Guelph
paragraphs: Above the Niagara Escarpment the bedrock changes. The escarpment is not a fault but the edge of a resistant cap of Silurian dolostone, the Lockport Group, on weaker shale that erodes from beneath it; the soft Clinton Group, including the Rochester Shale, undercuts the falls at Niagara, with Queenston shale below. Our Hamilton Mountain and Ancaster points returned Lockport Formation: thick-bedded limestone to dolostone, cherty dolostone and argillaceous dolostone with shale beds.

Guelph sits further up the same stack: its downtown point returned the Guelph Formation, tan to brown crystalline dolostone named for the city, under gravelly glaciofluvial deposits. Dolostone is harder than shale and the contact can be abrupt. Magnum's bulletin says end bearing on hard rock is common, usually on a single helix, but torque only verifies capacity where the transition is gradual or weathered; otherwise the engineer relies on adjacent logs or a load test. Guelph's deck page asks for the type, depth and size of piers.

sections.heading: Creek valleys and modern alluvium
paragraphs: Every creek that crosses the lake plain, from the Humber and Etobicoke Creek to the Credit, Sixteen Mile, Bronte and Forty Mile creeks, has laid down its own floor. The map calls this unit 19, modern alluvium, and unit 12, older alluvium: clay, silt, sand and gravel that may contain organic remains. Port Credit returned unit 19 and downtown Grimsby unit 12.

Alluvium is the least predictable ground on this page: loose sand over soft silt over gravel over shale within a few metres, and organic layers that carry little load. Report 257 warns that fine lake sands and silts may yield troublesome quantities of water during excavation and that bank stability is likely to be a problem near valleys. For a pile this usually means more extension sections.

sections.heading: Why the engineer's determination does not travel between neighbourhoods
paragraphs: Oakville's deck permit drawings say it directly: for steel helical piers or piles, a professional engineer must determine the depth, spacing and size based on soil condition, with the manufacturer's information and CCMC approval submitted with the application. Hamilton's deck and porch checklist asks for helical pier engineer-approved specifications and the Minister's Ruling or BMEC approval. Halton Hills requires drawings to show the depth, size, spacing and type of foundations.

The maps show why. In Oakville alone the surface flips from clay till to beach sand at the Lake Iroquois shoreline and to bare shale in the creek valleys, and the bedrock changes from Queenston to Georgian Bay across town. The Peel Region study for downtown Brampton found both formations in boreholes although the map shows only Queenston. Every pile carries its own torque log, and the engineer's sealed certificate of conformity rests on it.

sections.heading: Frost depth and adfreeze in these soils
paragraphs: The design figure we work to is 1.2 m, the minimum pier depth on Halton municipalities' deck drawings and the design frost depth in geotechnical reports filed with the Town of Oakville. Oakville's drawings print a minimum of 4 ft below grade on undisturbed soil, Halton Hills prints 1,200 mm, and two geotechnical reports on oakville.ca use 1.2 m. Hamilton's checklist asks only that pier depth be shown.

Frost acts on a pile in two ways, and the soil decides which matters. Heave is the soil expanding as pore water freezes; it needs water and a frost-susceptible soil, so a silty lake deposit over a shallow water table can heave a great deal while a well-drained gravel bar barely moves. Adfreeze is ice bonding to the shaft. In one winter comparison on stiff clay, a drilled concrete pier heaved about 36 mm, a helical pile about 5 mm.

The till and lake-clay areas of Peel, Halton and the Hamilton Mountain are where frost matters most, the Iroquois sands and escarpment gravels least. In both, the pile is screwed below the frost line and anchored by the helix, so resistance below the frost zone is designed to exceed the adfreeze pull. Frost movement is designed against, not eliminated. We install year-round; in frozen ground the frost crust is pre-drilled or thawed first, which adds time and can add cost.

sections.heading: What you can find out before you call
paragraphs: Three things are free and take an evening. First, your municipality's deck drawings: Oakville, Milton and Halton Hills publish sample drawings showing the pier depth, the footing table and the helical pile note, so you can see what the building department will ask for. Second, the OGS maps: the MRD 128-REV and MRD 219 services are public, and the query URLs in our sources return the unit at any coordinate.

Third, a neighbour's dig: a fence post, pool or sewer lateral on your street tells you where the till starts, whether water came in, and whether anyone hit rock. If a development near you filed a geotechnical report, it is often on the town's website with the planning application, as the two Oakville reports we cite are; Peel Region publishes desktop studies for its own works.

faqs.q: Is the ground under my house the same as the map says?
faqs.a: Usually, but the map is drawn at 1:50,000 and cannot show fill, a buried ravine or the disturbed strip beside a foundation. We use the OGS unit as the starting hypothesis and confirm it with the torque record as each pile goes in. The engineer's determination is for your lot.

faqs.q: What happens if the pile hits shale before it reaches its torque?
faqs.a: Rotation stops advancing, which the industry calls refusal. We record it in the log and the engineer decides: accept the pile on adjacent logs or a load test, back it out and re-advance, resize the helices, pre-drill a pilot hole the width of the shaft, or move the pile.

faqs.q: Why might a job in gravel need a load test?
faqs.a: CCMC report 13675-R states that where the pile is installed in granular material larger than 200 mm the torque-to-load relationship is not as predictable, and allowable loads must then be confirmed by on-site load tests under a geotechnical engineer holding a licence. Cobbly gravel on the Lake Iroquois shoreline is where that applies.

faqs.q: Does clay till hold a pile well?
faqs.a: Dense Halton Till is dependable ground: torque builds steadily and the pile reaches its design value without surprises. The top metre can be weathered and softer, and the lake silts that sometimes cover it are frost-susceptible, so the pile bears in dense till below the design frost depth.

We design to 1.2 m, the minimum pier depth on Halton municipalities' deck drawings and the design frost depth in geotechnical reports filed with the Town of Oakville. Hamilton's checklist asks that pier depth be shown without printing a figure, so we carry 1.2 m there.

faqs.q: Do you serve Toronto and Niagara?
faqs.a: Toronto and the Niagara municipalities from Grimsby to St. Catharines appear here because the same shale and Lake Iroquois deposits continue under them. Ask when you request a quote and we will confirm coverage and any minimum charge in the written quote.
